identification.title: I Surrender All
identification.artist: Judson W. Van DeVenter and Winfield S. Weeden
identification.notes: Words by Judson W. Van DeVenter (1855-1939), music by Winfield S. Weeden (1847-1908); first published in 1896 in Gospel Songs of Grace and Glory (Sebring Publishing, New York). Van DeVenter wrote it at George Sebring's home in East Palestine, Ohio, to mark his own decision to give his life to full-time ministry, after about five years of hesitation. Public domain. The list's guess of the hymn is right. It is widely recorded and was made familiar by Billy Graham's crusades, who studied under Van DeVenter; a fifth stanza is often omitted. Reviewed as the hymn as congregations sing it, not as any one recording.

claims.structuralNotes: Several short stanzas, each followed by the same refrain of full surrender. The stanzas run through the singer's commitments: to submit humbly to Jesus and trust him, to give up worldly pleasure and put him first, to be wholly his, to yield everything to his love, and to ask for the Holy Spirit's power and for being made whole in him. The voice is first person singular throughout and the subject is the singer's consecration. Christ and the Holy Spirit are named, and the song assumes that Christ is worthy of such devotion and has a claim on the singer, but it does not narrate the cross or resurrection; the gospel is the unspoken ground rather than the stated content.

claims.claim: The believer is to yield himself wholly and humbly to Jesus.
claims.subject: Consecration

claims.claim: Jesus is to be put above worldly pleasure and the singer's own way.
claims.subject: Devotion to Christ

claims.claim: The singer gives everything to Christ's love, trusting his care.
claims.subject: Trust and dedication

claims.claim: The Holy Spirit is asked for power and for the singer to be made whole.
claims.subject: The Spirit and sanctification

claims.claim: The singer asks to be made fully his, with the Spirit's power in life and witness.
claims.subject: Sanctification

strengths.title: Surrender as the Christian's whole posture
strengths.explanation: The hymn puts the call of total allegiance to Christ in a congregation's mouth: nothing held back, Christ first. It is the standing response of the redeemed rather than a means of earning anything.
strengths.scriptureRationale: Presenting the whole self as a living sacrifice in response to God's mercies - the consecration the refrain repeats.

strengths.title: Dependence on the Spirit for the surrendered life
strengths.explanation: One stanza asks the Holy Spirit for power, so the singer does not rest the life of surrender on resolve alone. That qualifies the song's own centre of gravity.
strengths.scriptureRationale: Walking by the Spirit rather than the flesh - the dependence the stanza voices.

doctrinesAffirmed: Lordship of Christ over the whole life
Consecration as the believer's response to grace
theological.assessment: No false statement. The hymn is a testimonial prayer of consecration and says nothing the Bible's call to total allegiance does not say. Its weakness is one of omission, recorded in the substance answers: it names no act of God, so the reason for surrender (the cross) is assumed rather than sung, and the singer's resolve is its subject. Taken alone it could be heard as a self-dedication without a gospel; sung with a song of the cross it is sound.

strengths.title: A response song with a long church life
strengths.explanation: Churches have used it as an invitation and a song of dedication for over a century, and its refrain is simple enough for a room to hold from memory.

strengths.title: A short, memorable refrain
strengths.explanation: The refrain is easy to learn, so a congregation can join on first hearing.

communal.vocalRangeNote: Commonly printed in the flat keys; a mid-range gospel melody that most mixed congregations manage. Check against the leader's key and the arrangement used.

range.key: Varies by hymnal; no key verified
range.note: No chart was read for this review, so the pitches are not stated.

communal.repetitionAssessment: A fixed refrain returns after each stanza and gathers the stanza's particular surrender into one confession.
communal.assessment: Strophic, congregational and easy to sing. It suits a response or consecration moment after the gospel has been preached or sung; its singular voice fits a prayer of commitment, though a room should not be asked to feel what the words do not give it ground to feel.

strengths.title: A single clear idea
strengths.explanation: The song says one thing and says it plainly, so there is little to misread.

clarity.assessment: Clear in what it asks. It does not say why Christ is worthy of surrender; a hearer unfamiliar with the gospel would not learn it from this song.

synthesis.summary: A 1896 gospel hymn of personal consecration: the singer yields everything to Jesus, puts him first, and asks the Holy Spirit's power. It makes no false statement and its voice is a testimonial prayer. It names no act of God, so the cross that grounds surrender is assumed, not sung.

scriptureReferences.relevance: Presenting oneself wholly to God in view of his mercies - the hymn's central act.
Denying oneself and following Christ daily - the call of full allegiance.
Walking by the Spirit - the dependence the Spirit stanza voices.

sources.title: I Surrender All
sources.establishes: Writers, 1896 Sebring publication, the East Palestine origin, the hymn's use as a dedication or invitation, and the often-omitted fifth stanza.

sources.title: I Surrender All
sources.establishes: Confirms authors, 1896 publication in Gospel Songs of Grace and Glory, and its popularising by Billy Graham.
